title: E45 - How to Get a Job at Legora, Harvey and Other Legal AI Startups, Kyle Poe, VP of Legal Innovation at Legora
author: Kyle Poe

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: The source focuses on legal-AI career paths, legal-engineering skills and movement between startups and law firms. It does not address in-house departments as AI buyers, selective insourcing, outside-counsel spending or the division of work between corporate legal teams and external providers.

st.t: Vendor value: Concentration forecasts face diverse competition
st.an: The source focuses on legal-AI employment opportunities and transferable technology skills rather than who captures durable vendor value, whether the market will concentrate, or how specialist vendors compare with competing models and tools. It therefore provides insufficient evidence to assess the cluster’s principal proposition.
qs: Very early in his career, he did a lot of tech work inside the firm that at the time probably wasn't all that popular, but it built a whole set of skills that have obviously come into play later in his career.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s client-outcome and multidisciplinary-delivery framing, treating technology development that solves client legal problems as legal practice. It materially extends the staffing discussion by identifying experienced associates who can translate practice knowledge into AI workflows as strong legal-engineer candidates, while offering only interview-based hiring observations rather than market-wide evidence.
qs: If the client has a legal problem that requires legal services from a law firm, and the work I'm doing is in direct service of solving that problem, that's legal work.

I think that's where this legal engineer role exists, where we're hiring probably the most aggressively, I think others are as well, is to bridge the gap between the legal tasks, like the practice skills that they learn after three to four years as an associate and doing things the old way.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: Poe accepts the cluster’s core view that technology creates legal value when embedded in client-facing practice rather than isolated as a separate innovation function. He materially extends it by treating technology building itself as legal practice whenever it directly solves a client’s legal problem, while his account of persistent scepticism illustrates the cultural barriers to institutional absorption.
qs: I never moved into an innovation role or knowledge management role, because for me, it was always about client service.
If the client has a legal problem that requires legal services from a law firm, and the work I'm doing is in direct service of solving that problem, that's legal work.

st.t: Repeatable services: Organisational redesign changes legal delivery
st.an: Poe accepts the broader redesign of legal delivery and materially extends it by treating client-focused technology development itself as legal practice, rather than as a separate innovation function. His contribution clarifies how practising lawyers’ roles may expand to include building the systems through which legal services are delivered, though he does not establish scalability or commercial outcomes.
qs: I never moved into an innovation role or knowledge management role, because for me, it was always about client service.
If the client has a legal problem that requires legal services from a law firm, and the work I'm doing is in direct service of solving that problem, that's legal work.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts that AI will commoditise routine production before displacing lawyers’ relational value, and materially extends the cluster by identifying legal engineering as a hybrid role that combines associate-level practice knowledge with AI-tool mastery to redesign legal workflows. Its claims are mainly experience-based forecasts rather than measured market-wide evidence.
qs: I think that's where this legal engineer role exists, where we're hiring probably the most aggressively, I think others are as well, is to bridge the gap between the legal tasks, like the practice skills that they learn after three to four years as an associate and doing things the old way.
And then the thing that's going to be like the last frontier is the relationships, right?

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: Poe accepts the cluster’s service-redesign framing and materially extends its account of professional identity: he treats client-serving technology development as legal practice itself, while reporting that others continued to distinguish it from “real” practice. This provides a concrete practitioner example of how role boundaries can impede multidisciplinary implementation, though it remains anecdotal.
qs: If the client has a legal problem that requires legal services from a law firm, and the work I'm doing is in direct service of solving that problem, that's legal work.
But when are you going to get back to practicing?

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Poe accepts the task-reallocation and work-redesign framing: routine production is expected to be automated first, while lawyers shift toward client relationships, management and broader professional skills. He materially extends the cluster by treating client-specific technology and workflow construction as legal work that may be billable, although his labour claims are predictions rather than empirical evidence and he does not address verification in depth.
qs: And so the grinders, that's the task that AI is going to handle first, right?
If the client has a legal problem that requires legal services from a law firm, and the work I'm doing is in direct service of solving that problem, that's legal work.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Poe supports the cluster’s emphasis on experience as a prerequisite for effective AI-enabled legal work: he argues that several years of associate practice provide practical knowledge law school does not, enabling lawyers to bridge legal tasks and technology. His hiring observations also reinforce the emerging legal-engineer role, though he does not directly assess whether automation is eroding apprenticeship or propose reconstructed training systems.
qs: But for people who are a couple of years of practice under their belt, they'll actually know what it is to be a lawyer, since law school doesn't really teach you this.

I think that's where this legal engineer role exists, where we're hiring probably the most aggressively, I think others are as well, is to bridge the gap between the legal tasks, like the practice skills that they learn after three to four years as an associate and doing things the old way.

st.t: Conditional optimism: User problems outrank AI branding
st.an: Poe supports the cluster’s conditional, risk-conscious outlook by treating legal-AI startup success as uncertain and prioritising transferable skills and career development over speculative valuation gains. His contribution is practical career guidance rather than evidence about adoption, reliability or market outcomes.
qs: But I think it's much more important to focus on one's own career development.

So I guess, I speak about being a lawyer, I'm thinking a little bit more risk averse about this, but I think it's important to focus on skills that will continue to employ you, even if the one particular company you work, if you were to go join a startup, even if they don't make it, you'll still be in a good position if they join another company, or again, go back to like practice, now upscale with AI powers.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Poe supports the cluster’s core view that generative AI broadens the legal tasks software can address and that durable value comes from workflow-specific product layers rather than chat alone. His tabular-review example and comparison with less-flexible predecessor tools reinforce the specialist-workflow thesis, although his evidence is experiential and demonstration-based and does not substantively address human verification or measured reliability.
qs: And what I knew at that time, kind of along the way was that there was very few, most legal problems did not have a technology solution before Genertip AI, right?

And there have been similar kind of predecessor technologies, like Chira Systems is kind of the most notable example, the firms that invested earlier on, where it was kind of more traditional machine learning that could do data extraction of contracts, but it required a huge amount of training data, a huge amount of pre-configuration.

kp.k: Practice-led technology development creates transferable innovation skills
kp.d: Poe describes beginning an internal technology project around 2013 in response to inefficient scaling and fragmented case information at Morgan Lewis. Working with IT and existing infrastructure, and later learning JavaScript and CSS when IT support receded, developed skills while he remained a practicing lawyer. His experience supports his recommendation that technology projects address immediate client-service problems while anticipating future needs; it is a personal account, not systematic evidence of career outcomes.
qs: So instead of being more efficient, we become less efficient as we were growing.
you have to solve an immediate pain point or else you're never going to get any traction.
But you also have to have an eye towards the future of future problems you can solve with this.
I never moved into an innovation role or knowledge management role, because for me, it was always about client service.

kp.k: Client-specific AI workflow development can constitute billable work
kp.d: Poe argues that prompting, learning tools and building workflows can be billable under hourly arrangements when directly solving a particular client's problem, unlike general-purpose learning. He frames this as a broader conception of legal practice centered on solving legal problems rather than conventional methods. This is his billing position, not a cited professional-rule determination or evidence of universal client acceptance.
qs: I think the time you spend learning the AI tools or learning any technology tools or building with those tools can be billable.
It's just kind of a fine line depending on whether or not there's any specific client problem that you're solving.
If you are just general purpose learning, you wouldn't be able to bill that to a client.

kp.k: Faster delivery exposes tensions between hours and client value
kp.d: Abramowitz reports unnamed firms reducing deliverable turnaround from weeks to days using AI, followed by questions from clients and billing partners about time actually spent. In his transactional example, speed helped make the deal possible, leading him to argue that reduced time can increase value. He raises, without resolving, whether prior technology research and development should enter the billing calculation.
qs: would have taken weeks, and the firm was able to get it done in days.
So speed here shouldn't have decreased the value, it should have increased.

should we count up all of the hours of R&D that our team did over the last year, like three years, looking at every product on the market, going out to conferences, meeting with vendors, trying their own hand at code?

kp.k: Generative AI expands technology beyond repeatable data-heavy practices
kp.d: Poe contrasts earlier technologies suited to his scalable litigation practice with generative AI's language capabilities, which he perceived as making technology relevant to a much broader range of legal problems. He says his desire to pursue AI intensively conflicted with initial law-firm caution and prompted a search outside the firm around 2023–2024. This is his account of a technological shift and career decision; the transcript's garbled percentages do not supply a reliable quantitative estimate.
qs: the database isn't going to help you do better appellate research and research writing.
Because again, computers learn to speak language for the first time.
This was around 2023, 2024 when I started looking.

kp.k: Tabular review offers scalable alternatives to conversational AI
kp.d: Poe recounts a demonstration of Legora's predecessor product in which a couple thousand contracts were loaded into tabular review for extraction of information such as parties and terms. He saw this as a new interaction model better suited to work at scale than question-and-answer chat. He contrasts it with earlier machine-learning extraction systems requiring extensive training data and configuration. These are demo-based observations and comparative judgments, not measured accuracy or productivity results.
qs: all AI had been up to this point was this question and answer chat interface experience
here's a new mode of interacting with AI in a scalable way that just really spoke for itself.
a couple thousand contracts were just dragged and dropped into the tabular review.
it required a huge amount of training data, a huge amount of pre-configuration.

kp.k: Legal engineers bridge practice knowledge and AI implementation
kp.d: Poe identifies legal engineering as a major hiring focus at Legora. Former associates translate practical legal tasks into effective use of AI tools and work directly with law-firm associates and partners during pre-sale pilots and post-sale implementations. He emphasizes experience acquired in practice rather than law school alone. This describes a software vendor's implementation role, not an alternative legal service provider delivering legal work.
qs: I think that's where this legal engineer role exists, where we're hiring probably the most aggressively
the practice skills that they learn after three to four years as an associate and doing things the old way.
we spend a large amount of resources both on pilots, pre-sale, as well as post-sale during implementations
these legal engineers on-site to work really like one-on-one hand-in-hand with fellow former associates or people who are currently associates, as well as partners.

kp.k: Vendor recruitment extends beyond mid-career associates
kp.d: Poe says the traditional legal-engineer recruitment range was three to seven years of experience, but Legora has hired people with one to two years and recently attracted senior practitioners and innovation professionals. At the interview, he describes himself as Legora's only former partner, while reporting offers to other former partners and interest from partners at major firms. He says direct law-school hiring is not yet occurring and predicts it may happen; these are company-specific recruitment claims.
qs: I think the traditional role was like three to seven year
we have hired some legal engineers who have the one to two-year experience.
Right now, I'm the only former partner here at Legora, but we've actually already made some offers to some other people who had been partners at various points in their career.
We're not quite hiring people straight out of law school, but probably well at some point.

kp.k: Career pivots require practical investment and active networking
kp.d: Poe attributes his eventual Legora move to conference encounters and continued discussions that shaped a role appropriate to his seniority. He advises qualified applicants not to stop at submitting a website application but to contact people directly. Abramowitz separately recommends developing technology skills inside firms, accepting possible trade-offs and actively pursuing opportunities rather than expecting an immediate transition from conventional billable practice.
qs: for me, it took a little bit longer to kind of go back and forth and define what the proper scope of the role would be.
I think probably the biggest mistake is just applying on a website and being done.
you're going to get so much further in the application process if you just reach out.
try to build as many skills as you can, like, within the context of your law firm

kp.k: AI startups offer intensive work with visible commercial impact
kp.d: Poe cautions that Legora is not a lifestyle alternative to Big Law: he compares its shared effort to trial preparation. He nonetheless finds the work more fulfilling because workflows and product contributions can visibly affect customers and secure deals, unlike litigation preparation that may never be used. He cites work on more end-to-end agentic workflows, including drafting an entire document from a term sheet, without supplying performance measurements or conditions for reliance.
qs: I would say this is not exactly a lifestyle company.
It reminds me of the days of preparing for trial where we're just all in the trenches together.
You help build a workflow that gets a multi-million dollar deal across the table.
particularly some of the stuff that's on the frontier of agentic AI, more end-to-end workflows, the ability to go from, say, a term sheet and draft the entire document.

kp.k: Automation may increase management and relationship skills' relative value
kp.d: Poe predicts that AI will first commoditize routine task execution, subsequently affect management, and leave relationships as a later frontier. He recommends networking, social skills and project management, warning that a career built only around narrow technical execution may become constrained or disappear. His expectation that relationships remain important for the next decade is a forecast, not a measured labor-market finding.
qs: as the AI commoditizes the doing of the grunt work of legal tasks, there's going to be other things in the pipeline that take on additional value.
So I very much encourage socializing with your peers, networking, project management.
the grinders, that's the task that AI is going to handle first
the thing that's going to be like the last frontier is the relationships
I mean, for the next decade, it'll still be.

kp.k: Trust and accountability sustain lawyers' value beyond commoditized work
kp.d: Abramowitz argues that client relationships are rational mechanisms for securing trusted work and continuing accountability, not merely arbitrary preferences. He recounts an unnamed partner acknowledging commoditized work while differentiating through an enjoyable working relationship. The host connects lawyers' continuing value to putting their names behind outcomes and professional insurance; this is his argument and anecdote, distinct from Poe's automation forecast.
qs: what you want when you hire an attorney is someone who you deeply know and trust
someone who is going to have to live with, like, the work product that they gave you.
we completely acknowledge that the work is commoditized and that you could work with anyone on this
I think a lot of what legal is about is saying like, I want someone like on the hook for this

kp.k: Vendor employment may accelerate skills and enable return pathways
kp.d: Poe argues that full-time work with AI tools at Legora accelerates skill acquisition compared with balancing technology adoption and conventional associate responsibilities. He advises lawyers remaining in firms to make tool proficiency part of their competencies and internal reputation. Acknowledging uncertainty, he anticipates some legal engineers remaining with the vendor, others returning to practice or starting AI-powered firms, and a substantial group entering law-firm innovation and knowledge-management roles.
qs: you get to make this your full-time job, right? You get to up-skill.
it would take probably a lot longer to get at a firm because you're having to balance all the other responsibilities of being an associate.
of course nobody knows how this all plays out and what the careers are all going to look like in the next couple of years.
There will be people who start their own AI-powered law firms.
a huge segment who goes in and does innovation and knowledge management type roles within firms

kp.k: Career development should outweigh speculative startup equity returns
kp.d: Abramowitz cites a recently announced five and a half billion dollar valuation and 550 million raised, while explicitly questioning whether Legora will justify its valuation. Poe points to investor expectations but stresses that valuation is paper wealth dependent on execution. Both recommend prioritizing learning and career development over equity upside; Poe presents portable AI skills as protection if a particular startup fails. No employee compensation figures or expected returns are established.
qs: five and a half billion dollar valuation announced recently on, what was it, 550 million raised.
I don't know if Legora is going to ultimately be worth what their current valuation is or not.
it's all paper money, right?
you see it as a bonus or the perk, something that would be great if it works out.
it's important to focus on skills that will continue to employ you

kp.k: Innovation pace and financial endurance underpin vendor competition
kp.d: Poe says Legora has no moat and argues that current feature-by-feature comparisons are less important than innovation trajectory because relative advantages can change within weeks. He presents capital raising partly as reassurance to customers that the company can compete and survive against heavily funded rivals capable of sustained losses. These are an executive's strategic claims about competition and customer confidence, not independent evidence of defensibility or future survival.
qs: what's your moat at Legora? And I'll say we don't have one, right? Like there is no moat.
But that could change in three weeks.
You want somebody who's going to be around in five or 10 years.
they can use that money to be inefficient, to lose money for a very, very long time if you have enough money.
I think that's one reason that we've raised so much is to assure our customers that we will be around.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Kyle Poe predicts broader technological applicability to legal work, expanding legal-AI careers, commoditization of routine tasks, and increasing relative value for management and relationships.
pts.d: Poe argues that generative AI changes the applicability of technology from relatively narrow, repeatable legal tasks to a much broader range of language-based work. The transcript's numerical description of that expansion is garbled, so no precise percentage is extracted. He describes Legora's tabular review as a scalable alternative to chat interfaces and contrasts it with earlier contract-extraction systems requiring substantial training data and configuration. He also describes emerging agentic workflows that can draft an entire document from a term sheet. On billing, Poe maintains that technology learning or workflow development directed at a specific client problem can constitute billable work under hourly arrangements, unlike general-purpose learning; this is his position rather than an independently established billing rule. He reports expanding demand at Legora for legal engineers who translate legal practice into AI implementations. He predicts that AI will commoditize routine execution first, increasing the relative importance of management, social skills, networking and client relationships, while careers built exclusively around narrow routine expertise may become limited or disappear. He argues that full-time work at a legal-AI startup accelerates AI skill acquisition and predicts subsequent career paths into AI-powered law firms, conventional practice, innovation and knowledge management. Regarding vendor competition, he says Legora has no moat and emphasizes execution, innovation speed and sufficient capital to remain competitive rather than current feature comparisons or paper valuations.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Poe principally supports his claims with personal practice, product-demonstration, hiring and implementation experience; broader forecasts are not supported by systematic measurements in this source.
pts.d: Poe draws on building a data platform while practising at Morgan Lewis, experimenting with generative AI, moving through a legacy technology company and joining Legora. His earlier platform-building experience supports his account of technology-enabled legal practice but is not itself evidence of generative-AI outcomes. His comparison of tabular review with older extraction technology rests on a demonstration involving roughly a couple thousand contracts and his knowledge of prior systems, not a comparative benchmark. His employment claims draw on firsthand reports of hiring associates with varying experience, offers to former partners, and interest from senior innovation and knowledge-management professionals. His account of startup impact includes workflows helping secure multimillion-dollar deals, without identifying transactions or separating their contribution from other factors. His valuation discussion invokes repeat and new investor participation and inferred investor expectations, rather than presenting financial models or guaranteed returns. The source offers no controlled productivity study, accuracy benchmark, employment dataset or quantified evidence for the predicted commoditization sequence, faster skill acquisition or future career distribution. Poe is a senior employee discussing his own company, and his positive assessments and predictions are attributed accordingly.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Poe distinguishes current hiring and implementation activity from uncertain career forecasts, a progressive automation sequence and an approximately decade-long role for relationships.
pts.d: The interview is framed as taking place in 2026. Poe dates his search outside the firm to around 2023–2024, says he joined Legora about seven months before the interview, and places its official US launch roughly a year earlier. Current legal-engineer recruitment traditionally targets approximately three to seven years of practice, with some hires having one to two years and increased senior interest in the preceding few months. He says Legora is not yet hiring directly from law school but probably will eventually; no date is specified. The automation sequence is conditional: routine execution goes first, management gains importance until AI can perform it, and relationships remain important for the next decade, although he leaves open their eventual erosion. Narrow-specialist career decline is conditional on AI learning to perform the relevant work better. He expects one or two years at legal-AI companies to equip some people for subsequent innovation roles, while expressly acknowledging uncertainty over the next few years. Startup equity upside depends on execution, continued growth and product development. Feature advantages may change within weeks, and customers are described as seeking vendors likely to remain available for five or ten years. Billability is conditional on work addressing a specific client matter rather than general education.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims chiefly concern law-firm lawyers, legal-AI vendor employees, law-firm clients and buyers choosing legal-AI platforms.
pts.d: Associates with practical legal experience are presented as candidates for legal-engineer roles bridging lawyers' tasks and AI tools. In this source, Legora recruits lawyers and former associates into those roles; the role title should not be read as evidence that its recruits are non-lawyers. Senior partners and innovation or knowledge-management staff also appear as potential entrants. Existing associates and partners receive hands-on support during pilots and implementations. Lawyers focused narrowly on routine execution face the career risks Poe predicts, while those developing relationship, management and AI implementation skills may gain relative value. Legal-AI employees can obtain faster skill development and more visible commercial or product impact, but Poe cautions that Legora is not a lifestyle employer and continues to demand substantial effort. Future beneficiaries may include firms hiring AI-experienced innovation professionals and lawyers establishing AI-powered practices. Clients are implicated through technology-enabled delivery and the proposed distinction between client-specific billable development and nonbillable general learning. Software buyers are described as assessing vendor durability alongside capabilities; startup employees are advised to prioritize transferable skills over uncertain equity upside. These are principally professional and enterprise-market claims, not claims about access to justice or unmet public legal need. Legora is discussed as a technology vendor, not as an alternative legal service provider.
